description: The deepest layer: truth, knowledge, reality, existence, nothing, meaning, cause, possibility, change, and form. Every path eventually arrives here, from many directions, so these concepts have the most links.

concepts.title: Truth
concepts.summary: What makes a statement right. Correspondence to the world, coherence with everything else we believe, usefulness: each theory captures something, and none has ended the argument.

concepts.title: Knowledge
concepts.summary: Belief that is true and has good reason behind it, or perhaps something subtler. Epistemology asks how we can know anything at all, and how sure we are entitled to be.

concepts.title: Reality
concepts.summary: What is there, whether or not anyone thinks so. Our access to it runs through senses, instruments, and theories, and the honest question is how much of what we see is the world and how much is our way of seeing.

concepts.title: Existence
concepts.summary: The plain fact that there is something rather than nothing. It's hard to say anything about it that isn't already presupposing it, which is probably why it stays so quietly astonishing.

concepts.title: Nothing
concepts.summary: The absence of anything at all, which turns out to be difficult to pin down. Physics's vacuum is full of activity, and philosophy asks whether nothing could even be, or only be imagined.

concepts.title: Emptiness
concepts.summary: In Buddhist thought, the idea that things have no fixed, independent essence and exist only through their relations. It isn't nothingness; it's what makes change and connection possible.

concepts.title: Meaning
concepts.summary: What makes a word, a gesture, or a life about something. It's neither found in the atoms nor simply invented; it seems to arise between minds, in use, and it is the thing most people are really asking about.

concepts.title: Causality
concepts.summary: The sense that things happen because of other things. Time seems to run one way, and causes come before effects, though the laws of physics themselves rarely distinguish cause from effect.

concepts.title: Determinism
concepts.summary: The view that everything follows from what came before. Classical physics leaned that way; quantum theory complicates it, and whether either leaves room for choice is the free will question again.

concepts.title: Possibility
concepts.summary: What could be but isn't yet, or isn't at all. It's how we plan, imagine, and regret, and philosophers still ask whether other possibilities are real or only ways of speaking.

concepts.title: Risk
concepts.summary: The chance of something going wrong, weighed against what you stand to gain. People are famously poor at feeling it accurately, which is why we count.

concepts.title: Impermanence
concepts.summary: Everything that arises passes away. Buddhist and Taoist thought build much of their practice on facing this squarely, and thermodynamics arrived at the same place by a different road.

concepts.title: The Good
concepts.summary: What we ought to do, and to want. Traditions disagree about whether it's about outcomes, duties, character, or care, and most people find they use a bit of each.

concepts.title: Forms
concepts.summary: Plato's idea that beyond every particular circle there is a perfect one, and that the particular things we see are imperfect copies. Mathematicians still often talk as if they were discovering such things rather than making them.

concepts.title: Abstraction
concepts.summary: Setting aside detail to see what is shared. Every word, number, and layer of software is an abstraction, and thinking well is mostly choosing which details you can afford to forget.

concepts.title: Relation
concepts.summary: A way things stand with respect to each other: greater than, parent of, connected to. Much of mathematics, and of this map, is about relations more than about things.
